subject: design
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Concept of the skill, Coverage, Method, Verification, Do NOT Use When) and standard IA practice (task-first grouping, placement by frequency/task-entry, single-canonical-home, user-language labeling, wayfinding, test against task scenarios).

cases.scenario: A documentation site has strong content but users repeatedly fail to find setup instructions. Setup, troubleshooting, billing, and admin-role pages are filed under per-product-feature categories that mirror the engineering team's modules.
cases.context: Support tickets are dominated by 'how do I get started' questions even though a setup page exists.
cases.question: How should the agent restructure the IA?
expected_flags: Names 'getting set up' as a top user task / primary entry point
Inventories existing content before moving anything
Regroups by user goal (a coherent setup hub) rather than by engineering modules
Adds cross-links and wayfinding from related pages to setup
Verifies against no-prior-knowledge task prompts
expected_fix_hints: Create a goal-based setup section and surface it as an obvious entry point
Cross-link troubleshooting and billing back to the canonical setup home
absent_signals: Do not keep mirroring the engineering module structure in the nav
Do not just rename pages without regrouping by goal

Surfaces this expected flag: Inventories existing content before moving anything.
Surfaces this expected flag: Regroups by user goal (a coherent setup hub) rather than by engineering modules.
Surfaces this expected flag: Adds cross-links and wayfinding from related pages to setup.
Surfaces this expected flag: Verifies against no-prior-knowledge task prompts.

Recommends this expected fix or action: Cross-link troubleshooting and billing back to the canonical setup home.
Avoids this false-positive or out-of-scope signal: Do not keep mirroring the engineering module structure in the nav.
Avoids this false-positive or out-of-scope signal: Do not just rename pages without regrouping by goal.

cases.scenario: A stakeholder insists a newly launched but rarely used feature must become a top-level navigation item 'because it is strategically important.'
cases.context: The top-level nav already has nine items and is getting hard to scan.
cases.question: How should the agent respond to the placement request?
expected_flags: Importance alone does not earn a top-level nav slot
Placement is governed by frequency of use and whether it is a genuine task entry point
Proposes a tab, section, filter, or cross-link as a better home
Notes that promoting everything dilutes the navigation's meaning
expected_fix_hints: Place the feature where its actual task-entry and frequency warrant
Trim or regroup the nine top-level items toward limited, predictable levels
absent_signals: Do not add it to top-level nav purely on stated importance
Do not keep growing the top-level nav unbounded

cases.scenario: An app shows the same 'API keys' content in three places: under Settings, under Developers, and on a Getting Started checklist. The copies have already drifted and users are unsure which is current.
cases.context: The team duplicated the content so it would be 'easy to find from anywhere.'
cases.question: How should the agent fix the structure?
expected_flags: Establishes a single canonical home for the API-keys content
Replaces the duplicate copies with cross-links to the canonical home
Names the cost of multiple homes: fragmented maintenance and unclear currency
Groups the content by the user goal it serves
expected_fix_hints: Designate one authoritative location and cross-link from the other two
absent_signals: Do not keep three independent copies in sync
Do not solve findability by duplicating content

cases.scenario: An admin tool labels its main sections 'Entities', 'Provisioning', and 'RBAC' — terms drawn directly from the backend domain model. New users cannot tell where to manage their team members.
cases.context: Engineers named the sections after the database tables and internal subsystems.
cases.question: How should the agent improve the IA?
expected_flags: Relabels sections in recognizable user language (e.g. 'Team', 'Access', 'Members')
Uses stable user nouns and avoids internal jargon
Groups by the goal the user is pursuing rather than the internal subsystem
Tests the labels against first-time users / task prompts
expected_fix_hints: Replace implementation-term labels with user-language labels
Validate label recognizability with no-prior-knowledge users
absent_signals: Do not keep backend-domain terms as primary navigation labels
Do not assume the team's vocabulary matches the user's

cases.scenario: Users drilling four levels deep into a settings tree report getting 'lost' — there is no breadcrumb, no indication of sibling options, and the only way back is the browser button.
cases.context: The nesting is logically correct but offers no orientation cues.
cases.question: How should the agent address the disorientation?
expected_flags: Adds wayfinding: current location, sibling options, next action, and an escape path
Ensures users can recover from a wrong turn without restarting
Reconsiders whether the levels are limited and predictable (flatten if too deep)
expected_fix_hints: Add breadcrumbs / location indicators and a clear back-to-anchor path
absent_signals: Do not rely on the browser back button as the only escape path
Do not leave deep trees without orientation cues

criteria.statement: Surfaces this expected flag: Adds wayfinding: current location, sibling options, next action, and an escape path.
Surfaces this expected flag: Ensures users can recover from a wrong turn without restarting.
Surfaces this expected flag: Reconsiders whether the levels are limited and predictable (flatten if too deep).
Recommends this expected fix or action: Add breadcrumbs / location indicators and a clear back-to-anchor path.
Recommends this expected fix or action: Flatten unnecessarily deep nesting.
Avoids this false-positive or out-of-scope signal: Do not rely on the browser back button as the only escape path.
Avoids this false-positive or out-of-scope signal: Do not leave deep trees without orientation cues.

cases.scenario: A PM asks the information-architecture owner to (a) define the controlled vocabulary and assignment rules for content categories, (b) rewrite the empty-state copy on the inbox, and (c) audit the keyboard/ARIA accessibility of the new nav.
cases.context: The team treats 'information architecture' as an umbrella for all structure, text, and classification work.
cases.question: How should the agent scope these requests?
expected_flags: Controlled vocabulary and assignment rules are out of scope — that is taxonomy-design
Empty-state wording is out of scope once structure is settled — that is microcopy
Keyboard/ARIA accessibility audit is out of scope — that is a11y
Offers the in-scope part: the grouping, placement, labeling, and wayfinding of the nav
expected_fix_hints: Redirect classification governance to taxonomy-design, copy to microcopy, and accessibility to a11y
Deliver the IA structure and labels, and verify_with task-analysis and a11y
absent_signals: Do not author the taxonomy's assignment rules here
Do not write the empty-state sentences or run the ARIA audit here

cases.scenario: A new workspace renders a navigation and dashboard that look coherent when populated but collapse into a confusing blank shell on day one, when no projects, data, or members exist yet.
cases.context: The IA was designed only for the steady-state, data-rich case.
cases.question: How should the agent handle the low-data case?
expected_flags: Treats empty and low-data states as part of the IA, not an afterthought
Ensures the structure still reads clearly and preserves wayfinding when sections are empty
Keeps top-task entry points visible and meaningful in the empty state
expected_fix_hints: Design the navigation/section structure to hold its shape with zero data
Surface the first meaningful task as an entry point in the empty state
absent_signals: Do not assume the populated layout is sufficient for the empty case
Do not let empty sections erase the structural cues
